title: Analysis: Wind and solar save UK from gas imports worth £5.9bn during Hormuz crisis - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief estimates record UK wind and solar output (41% of 2026 power vs 25% gas) has avoided £5.9bn of gas imports since the Hormuz crisis began, as UK gas prices hit 189p/therm in September 2026, the highest since 2022. Household gas bills are rising 33% while electricity bills rise only 4%, and the government is pushing to decouple power prices from gas.

insights.claim: Carbon Brief estimates that record UK wind and solar generation has avoided gas imports worth £5.9bn since the start of the Hormuz crisis (dated in the article to the outbreak of US-Iran war in February 2026).
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Quantifies renewables as an energy-security hedge with a direct balance-of-payments value during a supply shock.
insights.quote: The UK has avoided the need for gas imports worth £5.9bn since the start of the Hormuz crisis
insights.locator: The UK has avoided the need

insights.claim: UK wind and solar generation is up 14% year-on-year in 2026 to date, reaching record levels.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Sustained growth in clean output structurally reduces UK gas-for-power demand.
insights.quote: the UK has been generating record amounts of power from wind and solar, up 14% year-on-year

insights.claim: Gas-fired electricity generation in the UK is down nearly 10% year-on-year in 2026 to date, which Carbon Brief attributes directly to record clean-power output.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Falling gas burn in power weakens a key demand leg for UK gas and LNG imports.
insights.quote: directly cutting the need for gas-fired electricity, which is down by nearly 10% year-on-year in 2026 to date

insights.claim: Wind and solar supplied a record 41% of UK electricity in 2026 to date, versus 25% from gas.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Renewables are now the dominant UK power source, shifting marginal economics of the grid.
insights.quote: wind and solar have generated a record 41% share of the UK’s electricity needs in 2026 to date, compared with 25% from gas

insights.claim: The gas imports avoided by UK wind and solar since the crisis began are equivalent to more than 100 additional LNG tanker deliveries.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Fewer UK LNG cargo needs reduces UK competition in a tight global LNG market.
insights.quote: the equivalent of more than 100 additional tanker deliveries of liquefied natural gas (LNG)

insights.claim: In September 2026 to date, UK wind and solar produced nearly 10 TWh, a record, which combined with surging gas prices yielded a £1.3bn gas import saving for the month.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The value of each renewable MWh scales with gas prices, so savings accelerate as the crisis deepens.
insights.quote: The £1.3bn import saving in September 2026 to date is the result of record wind and solar output, at nearly 10 terawatt hours (TWh)

insights.claim: UK wholesale gas averaged 90p per therm from 2023 until the start of 2026, roughly three times 2019 pre-Covid and pre-Ukraine levels, having stayed elevated since Russia cut supplies to Europe in 2022.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Shows UK gas has had a structurally higher price floor since 2022, even before the Hormuz shock.
insights.quote: Gas averaged 90p per therm from 2023 until the start of this year, roughly three times above 2019 prices

insights.claim: Since war broke out in the Middle East, UK gas prices have averaged 134p per therm, nearly four times 2019 levels, and in September 2026 averaged 189p per therm, the highest since the 2022 energy crisis.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Gas prices are back to crisis-era levels, raising costs for gas-dependent utilities, industry and households.
insights.quote: In September 2026 to date, gas prices have averaged 189p per therm, reaching their highest level since the global energy crisis in 2022

insights.claim: UK gas prices are spiking again because winter heating demand is approaching and there is no end in sight to the Hormuz crisis.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Seasonal demand plus an unresolved supply disruption points to continued upward pressure into winter.
insights.quote: UK gas prices are spiking again because winter is approaching
insights.locator: UK gas prices are spiking again

insights.claim: Low European gas stocks mean Europe will have to compete with Asia for LNG cargoes needed for winter heating.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Europe-Asia bidding competition supports elevated global LNG prices and benefits LNG sellers and shippers.
insights.quote: European gas stocks are low. This means Europe will have to compete with Asia to secure the cargoes of LNG
insights.locator: At the same time, European gas

insights.claim: Under Ofgem's price cap from 1 October 2026, typical UK household gas bills will be 33% (about £200 per year) higher than in April, while electricity bills will have risen only 4%, according to Nesta.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Divergent gas vs power bill inflation strengthens the economic case for electrification of heat and transport.
insights.quote: typical household gas bills will be 33% higher than they were in April, some £200 per year

insights.claim: Nesta attributes the muted rise in UK electricity bills to growing generation from clean-energy sources, arguing the link between electricity and gas prices has begun to break.
insights.speaker: Andrew Sissons
insights.so_what: If power prices decouple from gas, UK electricity becomes a less volatile input cost, favouring electrified demand.
insights.quote: “the link between electricity and gas prices has already begun to break”

insights.claim: UK prime minister Andy Burnham said he has asked energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to speed up breaking the link between domestic power prices and the international gas market, citing a massive expansion of home-grown renewables and nuclear.
insights.speaker: Andy Burnham
insights.so_what: Signals likely UK policy/market-design reform to decouple power prices from gas, relevant to generators, renewables and nuclear investors.
insights.quote: I have asked Miatta to speed up the breaking of the link between what we pay for power at home and the international gas market

insights.claim: UK energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said energy bills are high because the UK is exposed to global fossil-fuel markets.
insights.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
insights.so_what: Government framing of fossil-fuel exposure as the problem supports continued pro-renewables policy.

insights.claim: The EU has reportedly paid an extra €100bn for fossil-fuel imports since the start of the crisis, with higher import bills hitting low and middle-income countries particularly hard.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Large terms-of-trade shock for fossil importers, with macro stress concentrated in emerging importers.
insights.quote: The EU has reportedly had to pay an extra €100bn for fossil-fuel imports since the start of the crisis

insights.claim: UK diesel prices have hit record levels of around £2 per litre, while Carbon Brief analysis finds electric cars up to nine times cheaper to drive.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A widening running-cost gap strengthens the consumer case for EV adoption during the oil shock.
insights.quote: diesel prices have hit record levels of around £2 per litre
